title: Quantifiers: how many times, and greedy vs lazy
explanation:
A **quantifier** says how many times the item just before it may repeat. The item can be one character, a class, or a group:

| Quantifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x*` | 0 or more |
| `x+` | 1 or more |
| `x?` | 0 or 1 (optional) |
| `x{n}` | exactly n |
| `x{n,}` | at least n |
| `x{n,m}` | between n and m |

By default quantifiers are **greedy**: they take as many repetitions as possible and give some back only if the rest of the pattern would otherwise fail. Put `?` after a quantifier (`*?`, `+?`, `{n,m}?`) to make it **lazy**: it stops at the minimum that lets the match succeed.

```js
const quote = 'say "hi" and "bye"';
console.log(quote.match(/".*"/)[0]);    // "hi" and "bye"   (greedy: runs to the last quote)
console.log(quote.match(/".*?"/)[0]);   // "hi"             (lazy: stops at the first closing quote)
```

A quantifier applies only to the single item before it: `ab+` means "a, then one or more b". To repeat a longer piece, group it first: `(?:ab)+`.
keyIdeas: Greedy is the default: as many as possible, backing off if needed.
A trailing `?` makes a quantifier lazy (as few as possible).
Quantifiers bind to one item; group to repeat more.

workedExample.problem: Validate prices: a whole number, optionally followed by a dot and **one or two** decimal digits. `"3"`, `"3.5"`, and `"12.50"` pass; `"3."`, `"3.555"`, and `".5"` fail.
steps: At least one digit before the dot: `\d+`.
The decimal part is optional as a whole, so group it and make the group optional: `(?:\.\d{1,2})?` — the dot is escaped to be literal.
Anchor both ends so nothing extra can sneak in: `^\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?$`.
workedExample.answer: `/^\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?$/` — `+` requires a whole part, `{1,2}` limits the decimals, and `?` makes the decimal part optional.

pitfalls: Using `.*` between delimiters and swallowing everything up to the *last* delimiter (greedy).
Writing `ab+` when you meant "repeat ab" — the `+` applies only to `b`.
Using `*` where at least one is required, so the empty string matches.

citations.quote: Matches the preceding item "x" 0 or more times.
Matches the preceding item "x" 1 or more times.
matches at least "n" and at most "m" occurrences of the preceding item "x".
By default quantifiers like * and + are "greedy", meaning that they try to match as many times as possible.
The ? character after the quantifier makes the quantifier "non-greedy": meaning that it will stop as soon as it finds the minimum number of matches.
If later portions of the pattern don't match, the matching engine will then back up and try again with fewer repetitions.
